<!-- Generated by the Kibitz release from its setup guide; edits here are replaced on the next release. -->

# Set up Kibitz

This page takes you from a new Mac to a project where Kibitz opens pull
requests and merges them. It follows the desktop app's first-run wizard screen by screen. You need no terminal and no file edits.

The numbered sections below match the wizard's steps, in the same order and
with the same names. A button or label in bold quotes is spelled exactly as
the wizard shows it.

## Before you start

- A Mac with Apple silicon.
- A GitHub account, and the repositories Kibitz may work in. A test
  repository is the best first one; you can also add them after setup.
- An account for the models: an OpenRouter account, or a Claude, ChatGPT or
  Google subscription.

## Install the app

Install the Kibitz desktop app with one line in Terminal:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://usekibitz.com/install | sh
```

It downloads the signed app, checks it, puts it in Applications and opens it.
No Homebrew needed. On a new install, which knows no server
yet, the app opens the wizard **"Set up Kibitz"**. Its steps are listed on the
left, and the one you are on is marked.

You can leave at any time. **"Finish setup later"** closes the wizard, and
**"Back"** returns to the step before. The wizard remembers its step, so if
you quit the app halfway it opens where you stopped.

The same line installs Kibitz on Debian, Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi OS (then
`sudo kbz setup`).

## 1. Choose this Mac's role

The screen asks **"What does this Mac do?"** and offers three roles:

- **"This is my Kibitz"**: the Kibitz server runs on this Mac. It works on
  your repositories, and your other apps and devices connect to it. Choose
  this for a first install. The rest of this page assumes it.
- **"Connect this device to my Kibitz"**: this Mac is a device of a Kibitz
  that runs on another computer, which can then show and drive it. You add it
  there, in Settings → Devices.
- **"Just the app"**: this Mac only runs the app, connected to a Kibitz
  elsewhere. Nothing runs here in the background.

Choose one and press **"Continue"**. You can change the role later in
Settings → This Mac, with nothing to reinstall.

## 2. Allow computer use

The screen **"Let Kibitz see and use this Mac"** lists the two macOS
permissions sessions need to take screenshots and click and type in your apps,
each with its live state. They are the same two Claude, ChatGPT and Codex ask
for, and Kibitz asks for nothing more:

- **Screen Recording**, for screenshots. macOS applies it once Kibitz is quit
  and reopened; setup comes back to this step. On macOS 15 and later, the
  first screenshot after that, and one now and then later, shows "Kibitz is
  requesting to bypass the system private window picker and directly access
  your screen and audio". Allow it: macOS asks this of every app that takes
  screenshots without its window picker, Claude included, and an agent cannot
  use the picker.
- **Accessibility**, to click, type, press keys and scroll.

Kibitz never needs **App Management**. Its own updates replace only its own
app, signed by the same developer, which macOS allows without it, and the
browser it drives runs as its own app, so Chrome's updater is never Kibitz's
(see [Mac computer use](mac-computer-use.md#what-kibitz-never-asks-for)).

Press each button, such as **Open Accessibility settings**: Kibitz asks
macOS first, so it is already in the list of the System Settings pane that
opens, and you only turn its switch on. The list updates by itself. Press
**"Continue"** when all are allowed, or **"Continue without them"** to set
them later in Settings → This Mac, which shows the same list; until then the
app shows a line saying which one is missing.

The other two roles then leave the wizard for Settings → Connection, where you
pair with your server.

## 3. Install Kibitz

The screen **"Install Kibitz on this Mac"** first checks the Mac:

- that it can run the Kibitz server;
- that Git is installed. Git comes with Apple's command line tools. If they are
  missing, press **"Install command line tools"**, follow Apple's installer,
  then press **"Check again"**;
- whether a Kibitz server already runs here.

Press **"Install Kibitz"**. The app installs the server it carries and starts
it in the background, where it starts again by itself each time you log in.
Its settings and data live in your home folder, in `~/.glm-console`. A new Mac
needs nothing else: the app brings its own runtime and Claude Code.

When a Kibitz server already runs on this Mac, the button reads **"Use the
server on this Mac"** and connects to it instead of installing a second one.
To pair with a server on another computer, use **"Connect to a server you
already run instead"**.

## 4. Connect GitHub

Kibitz opens pull requests and merges them as your GitHub account. You sign in
on github.com, and no password or token passes through Kibitz.

1. Press **"Sign in with GitHub"**. The first time, this also installs the
   GitHub CLI, which does the sign-in.
2. The wizard shows a short code. Press **"Copy code and open GitHub"**,
   paste the code on the page that opens, and approve Kibitz.
3. The wizard shows the account you signed in as. Press **"Continue"**.

If the code runs out before you approve, press **"Get a new code"**. If Kibitz
needs a permission your sign-in lacks, the screen names it: press **"Sign in
again"** to grant it.

## 5. Choose a model

Kibitz's agents run on a model you sign in to. Pick one way:

- **OpenRouter**, one account for models from many companies, paid as you use
  them. Press the button to sign in with OpenRouter and approve Kibitz in your
  browser. The wizard continues by itself when you have.
- **A subscription.** Open **"Or sign in with a subscription"** and sign in to
  the Claude, ChatGPT or Google subscription you have.

Approving on your phone or another computer? Open **"Approving on your phone
or another device?"**, press **"Copy the sign-in link"** and open it there.
That browser cannot come back to this Mac, so copy the whole address of the
page it ends on, paste it into **"The address the browser ended on"**, and
press **"Finish sign-in"**. If the link expires first, press **"Try again"**
for a fresh one.

Then pick **"The model every session starts on"** and press **"Continue"**.
The wizard suggests one, a Claude Sonnet where it can. You can change it, and
choose one per kind of session, in Settings → Models & effort schedule.

## 6. Name your assistant

Your assistant is the one conversation that works across every project: ask it
anything, or hand it work for any of them. It is yours to name; every install
starts with the plain default, "Assistant".

Type a name in **"Name"** and press **"Continue"**. Leave the field empty, or
press **"Skip"**, to keep the default. The sidebar, the home screen and the
messages it sends into other sessions all use the name you choose. You can
rename it any time in Settings → Assistant.

## 7. Choose what agents may do

The screen **"What may agents do without asking?"** asks once how much agents
may do on their own. Pick one and press **"Continue"**:

- **"Conservative"**: every click, keystroke and scroll on a computer asks you
  first, and the sandbox asks for anything outside its rules.
- **"Balanced"** (suggested): agents use computer control and Kibitz's own
  tools without asking. Writes outside the project, unlisted network hosts,
  secrets, sudo, destructive pushes and spending still ask.
- **"Full access"**: no prompts at all; agents run with no sandbox.

The preset sets both the computer-use approvals and the sandbox permissions.
Settings → Permissions shows which one you are on (or Custom, once you change
a single switch there) and switches it any time.

## 8. Add projects

The screen **"Add your projects"** explains how Kibitz is organized. Kibitz
works in projects: a project is one GitHub repository, with its own
orchestrator. You tell a project's orchestrator what to change, and it opens a
pull request for every change. Kibitz works in a copy of each repository on
this Mac.

You can add one repository here, several, or none:

1. Search **"Repository"** for one of yours, or type `owner/name` or its
   GitHub address. The list holds your own repositories, ones you collaborate
   on, and your organizations' repositories, most recently changed first;
   **"Owner"** narrows it to one account or organization.
2. Choose **"How changes land"** (see below).
3. Press the button to add the repository. Kibitz clones it and makes it a
   project with the repository's name. Picking a repository a project already
   works in reuses that project.
4. Press **"Add another repository"** to add the next one the same way, or
   **"Continue"** when you have added them all.

To start with no project, press **"Add projects later"** instead of picking
one. Once you have added some, the same button reads "Continue with" and how
many you have.

After setup, add a project at any time with **"Add project"**: the folder
button beside the project list in the sidebar, or **"Add project…"** in its
**"Project actions"** menu (the … button). It opens the same repository picker
as this step.

When an organization you belong to shows none of its repositories, the step
says why under the list:

- **Single sign-on**: the organization uses SAML SSO and your GitHub sign-in
  is not authorized for it. Open the GitHub CLI's page in your GitHub settings
  (the step's **"Open GitHub"** button), press **Authorize** beside the
  organization, then come back to the step.
- **App approval**: the organization restricts which apps may read its data
  and has not approved the GitHub CLI, which Kibitz signs in with. Press
  **Request** beside the organization on the same page, or ask one of its
  owners to approve it.

Typing `owner/name` still works for any repository you can clone.

### Can Kibitz land work there?

Once the repository is added, the step checks that the GitHub sign-in Kibitz
pushes, opens pull requests and merges with can actually land work in it. Each check shows as passed, missing (with its fix), or not checked
when an earlier one decides it or it does not apply:

- **Signed in to GitHub**: Kibitz still has a GitHub sign-in on this Mac.
  Missing: connect GitHub again in step 4.
- **Single sign-on**: when the organization requires SAML SSO, your sign-in is
  authorized for it. Missing: press **"Open GitHub"** (the **Authorize for
  SSO** page GitHub names), sign in to the organization's identity provider,
  press **Authorize**, then **"Check again"**.
- **App approved by the organization**: the organization's third-party access
  restrictions do not block the GitHub CLI, which Kibitz signs in with.
  Missing: ask an org owner to approve the app. Press **Request** beside the
  organization on the page **"Open GitHub"** shows; an owner then approves it
  in the organization's own GitHub settings, under **Third-party access**.
- **Repository visible**: GitHub shows the repository to your account.
  Missing: check the name, or ask one of its admins to add you.
- **Push access**: your role there is Write, Maintain or Admin. Missing ("you
  have read-only access", or the repository is archived): ask an admin of the
  repository for the Write or Maintain role, or pick another repository.
- **Trial branch push**: a `git push --dry-run` of a branch from the copy on
  this Mac is accepted. A dry run sends nothing: no branch or pull request is
  left behind. It is not checked for an empty repository.

**"Continue"** and **"Add another repository"** wait until every check
passes. If you want to go on anyway,
tick **"Continue anyway"**: Kibitz still can't push or open pull requests
there until the fix is made. You can run the same checks later from the
project's menu (**GitHub access in** and the project's name), which tries the
push from that project's own folder. A repository added after setup with
**"Add project"** is checked the same way.

Once a repository is added, the wizard offers **"Set up automatic merges…"**:
it shows exactly what Kibitz would change in the repository so its pull
requests merge once they pass, and changes nothing until you press **"Approve
and set up"**. You can skip this now and do it later from the project.

### How changes land

Every change a worker makes arrives as a pull request. This setting decides
what has to pass before Kibitz merges it:

- **"Local verify only"** (the wizard's choice on a single Mac): no CI. The
  server runs the repository's own checks on this Mac and merges on green.
  Nothing more is needed.
- **"GitHub-hosted runners"**: pull requests merge once their CI passes on
  GitHub's machines. Use it for a repository whose workflows already run there.
- **"Self-hosted runners"**: pull requests merge once their CI passes on your
  own runners. Use it only if you run GitHub Actions runners yourself.

You can change it per project later. When no runner can take a check the
repository requires, the merge setup says so, rather than letting the check
wait forever.

## 9. Add integrations (optional)

Kibitz works without any of these. Each is a card with its own steps. Connect
one now, or later in Settings → Integrations, where the same cards stay.

- **Push notifications**: alerts on your iPhone when a session finishes or
  needs you, with an APNs key from your Apple developer account.
- **Phone calls**: Kibitz calls you when something needs you now, through your
  own Twilio account.
- **1Password**: agents save new logins to one vault, and read the references
  you give them, through a service account that sees that vault alone.
- **Gmail**: Kibitz sends the emails you approve on a card from your Gmail,
  word for word.

Press **"Continue"** when you are done, whether or not you connected any.

## 10. Start working

Each project has an orchestrator. Tell it what you want changed, and it starts
a worker on its own branch. The worker's pull request lands the way you chose
in step 7, and you see each step in the session.

Press **"Open the orchestrator"** and ask for something small first, such as
"Add a short description to the README". The wizard closes, and the
orchestrator's session opens. With several projects it opens the first one
you added; each of the others has its own orchestrator in the sidebar.

If you added no project in step 7, the screen says where to add one, and
**"Finish setup"** closes the wizard.

## After setup

- **"Add project"** (the folder button beside the sidebar's project list): a
  repository as a new project, with its own orchestrator.
- Settings → Connection: the server this app talks to.
- Settings → This Mac: this Mac's role, and the permissions computer use needs.
- Settings → Assistant: your assistant's name.
- Settings → Models & effort schedule: models per kind of session.
- Settings → Integrations: the cards from step 8.
- Settings → Devices: other computers this Kibitz can show and drive.

The wizard does not set up the iPhone app yet.

A second Kibitz install, such as one on a work laptop, shares nothing with this
one unless you link them.

### What workers can reach on the network

Workers run their commands in a sandbox. By default a sandboxed command
reaches only the Kibitz server and this Mac's own `localhost`. Workers don't
need GitHub to push, open pull requests or merge: the Kibitz server does that
itself, outside the sandbox, with the GitHub sign-in from step 4. Package
installs, docs and other APIs are blocked until you allow their hosts.

Each project has its own list, and it applies to that project's sessions only.
To change it, open the project's menu, choose **Edit …**, and use
**Network access**:

- Tick **GitHub**, **npm** or **PyPI** to add the hosts those need.
- Or type hosts, one per line: `api.github.com`, or `*.example.com` for every
  subdomain of `example.com`.

On the iPhone, the same list is under the project's **Edit**. Apps and scripts
use `PATCH /projects/<id>` with `{"networkAllow": ["api.github.com"]}`, and
only with the owner's token: a session can never widen its own sandbox.

When a worker's command is blocked, its session says which host was blocked
and asks you on a card: **Allow for this session**, **Always allow in
<project>** (which adds the host to the project's list) or **Don't allow**.
The assistant and orchestrators ask on their own card instead: **Allow once** or
**Always allow**, which allows the host for every session on the server. A session's engine takes a new list as soon as it is idle, on the
same conversation.

`GLM_CONSOLE_ALLOW_DANGEROUS=1` still turns the sandbox off for every session
on the server. Prefer the project's list.
